newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: RICHEMONT MULLS MORE TV STAKES IN FUTURE.
newsitem.headline: RICHEMONT MULLS MORE TV STAKES IN FUTURE.

text.p: Johann Rupert, managing director for Swiss-based Compagnie Financiere Richemont AG, said that the tobacco, luxury goods, and media group was considering further investments in pay television in the future.
But, in an interview with Reuters Financial T.V., he said the group planned to hold onto its cash for the moment.

"We are in pay television, and non-news distributing pay television, entertainment. We are happy with our involvement, and as the cash flows build up in our Richemont group, we are looking to extend further investments in that area," he said.

Asked where the group might expand in future, Rupert said: "If I knew, I wouldn't tell you. I think the markets are very very high, they are skittish. If I look at smart investors in many parts of the world, they are looking at building up some liquidity for the downturn that will inevitably follow.
"With the Dow and the FTSE both at record levels, I think we would be looking at preserving cash for a while," he said.

In a deal announced in September, Canal Plus agreed to buy 100 percent of pay-television group NetHold BV from Richemont and MIH Holdings Ltd for $45 million cash and 6.1 million new Canal Plus shares.
Rupert said the deal was going according to plan and that a definitive accord giving Richemont a 15 percent stake in Canal Plus was set to be signed on December 12.
On other subjects, Rupert said Richemont was cautious about prospects for Rothmans International, the vehicle for its tobacco interests, whose growth was being weighed on by the strong pound.
"We have seen quite a bit of buying-in ahead of the budget in the U.K. but things are going according to track and according to plan for the long-term business," he said.

"We are satisfied with the performance in the first six months, although in sterling terms obviously we are suffering," he said, adding sterling's performance would play a large role in second-half results.

Rothmans operating profit rose 51.9 percent in the half to 401.1 million sterling. This relected a 12.3 percent rise in underlying tobacco operating profit and was helped in particular by the January merger with Rembrandt Group's tobacco business.

Rupert said production of luxury goods in hard-currency countries also presented a problem. Operating profit from the Vendome Luxury Group slipped 2.6 percent in the half to 110.4 million sterling but was largely steady in Swiss franc terms.
"Unfortunately, once again we have a currency scenario inasmuch as we are producing a majority of our goods in hard currency," he said, noting watches were made in Switzerland.

"Even though the Swiss franc may have weakened somewhat against sterling, the trend for the Swiss franc and the D-mark against third-party currencies has remained strong...As our costs are incurred in hard currencies for both the pens and the watches, again, we have a bit of currency problem," he said.
